reason: Under the Data Lifecycle Manager considerations, the quote states verbatim that when fast snapshot restore is enabled for a snapshot it takes 60 minutes per TiB to optimize the snapshot.

Under Pricing and Billing, the quote gives the example of one snapshot in US-East-1a for 30 days billed $540 as 1 snapshot x 1 AZ x 720 hours x $0.75 per hour, matching both values and the example scope.
The quote states that a volume created from a snapshot enabled for fast snapshot restore is fully initialized at creation and immediately delivers its full performance.

Under gp2 volume performance, the quote states gp2 volumes smaller than 1 TiB provisioned with less than 3,000 IOPS can burst to 3,000 IOPS when needed for an extended period; the context says bursting is governed by I/O credits.
Under gp2 volume performance, the quote states an I/O credit accrual limit of 5.4 million I/O credits, enough to sustain the maximum burst of 3,000 IOPS for at least 30 minutes.
Under gp2 volume performance, the quote states that when I/O demand drops to baseline or lower the volume earns 3 I/O credits per GiB of volume size per second.
The quote states gp2 volumes provide single-digit millisecond latency and 99.8 to 99.9 percent durability with an AFR no higher than 0.2 percent.
In the gp2 performance section, the note states each volume receives an initial balance of 5.4 million I/O credits, which provides a fast initial boot cycle for boot volumes.
Under gp2 volume performance, the quote states baseline IOPS scales linearly between a minimum of 100 and a maximum of 16,000 at 3 IOPS per GiB of volume size.
The quote states volumes 5,334 GiB and larger are provisioned with 16,000 IOPS, and the context names 16,000 as the gp2 maximum.
Under gp2 volume performance, the quote states volumes 33.33 GiB and smaller are provisioned with the minimum of 100 IOPS.
The first quote states that with gp2 performance scales with volume size; the second gives the linear 3 IOPS per GiB rate between 100 and 16,000.
Under gp2 volume size, the quote states a gp2 volume ranges from 1 GiB to 16 TiB and that performance scales linearly with size.
Under the gp2 pricing example, the quotes state I/O is included in the price of the volumes and the example uses a region that charges $0.10 per GB-month; the claim keeps the example-Region scope.
Under gp2 throughput performance, the quote states volumes 170 GiB and smaller deliver a maximum throughput of 128 MiB/s.
Under gp2 throughput performance, the quote states volumes 334 GiB and larger deliver 250 MiB/s.
The quote states gp2 volumes deliver throughput between 128 MiB/s and 250 MiB/s depending on volume size.
In the gp3 section, the quote states gp3 volumes offer a 20 percent lower price per GiB than gp2; the gp2 tip says up to 20 percent for prices in general, but the per-GiB statement is flat.
Under gp3 IOPS performance, the quote states a consistent baseline of 3,000 IOPS included with the price of storage; the context says additional IOPS cost extra.
Under gp3 throughput performance, the quote states a consistent baseline of 125 MiB/s included with the price of storage; the context says additional throughput costs extra.
The quote states that in the console, for creating a volume or an AMI from a snapshot, gp3 is the default selection, and that in other cases gp2 is the default selection.
The quote states gp3 volumes provide 99.8 to 99.9 percent durability with an AFR no higher than 0.2 percent, a maximum of two failures per 1,000 running volumes over a year.
Under the gp3 pricing example, the quote uses a region that charges $0.005 per provisioned IOPS-month, and the next context line applies it to IOPS above the 3,000 IOPS free baseline.
The quote states gp3 volumes provide single-digit millisecond latency.
The quote states gp3 volumes are the latest generation of General Purpose SSD volumes and the lowest cost SSD volume offered by Amazon EBS.

The guide quote gives up to 80,000 IOPS at 500 IOPS per GiB, reached at 160 GiB; the What's New post dated Sep 26, 2025 gives the previous 16,000 IOPS limit; the context places the Outposts limits in a separate note.
The quote states maximum IOPS can be provisioned for volumes 160 GiB or larger; the 500 IOPS per GiB ratio in the context means smaller volumes cannot reach 80,000, which supports the word only.
Under gp3 volume size, the quote states 1 GiB to 64 TiB; the What's New post dated Sep 26, 2025 states the previous limit was 16 TiB; the context gives the Outposts exception.
The guide quote gives additional throughput up to 2,000 MiB/s at 0.25 MiB/s per provisioned IOPS; the What's New post dated Sep 26, 2025 gives the previous 1,000 MiB/s limit.
The quote states maximum gp3 throughput can be provisioned at 8,000 IOPS or higher and 16 GiB or larger.
The note states that on Outposts gp3 volumes support sizes up to 16 TiB, IOPS up to 16,000 and throughput up to 1,000 MiB/s.
The quote states AWS designs gp3 volumes to deliver their provisioned performance 99 percent of the time.

In the gp3 section, the quote states this volume type helps you scale performance independently of volume size without provisioning additional block storage; the IOPS-per-GiB condition only narrows the claim and is stated on the same page.

In the gp3 block of the volume types page, the quote lists 3,000 IOPS free and $0.005 per provisioned IOPS-month over 3,000, and 125 MB/s free and $0.04 per provisioned MB/s-month over 125 MiBps; the $0.06 cross-reference matches the sibling pricing-page quote in this batch.
Under the gp3 pricing example, the quote uses a region that charges $0.08 per GB-month; the claim keeps the example-Region scope.

Under the gp3 pricing example, the quote uses $0.06 per provisioned MB/s-month, applied in the context to MB/s above the 125 MB/s free baseline; the $0.04 cross-reference matches the volume types quote in this batch.
Under the gp3 heading, the Use Cases line lists virtual desktops, medium sized single instance databases, low-latency interactive apps, dev and test, and boot volumes.
Under Service limitations, the quote states that with GPT boot volumes can be up to 64 TiB when used with GRUB2 (Linux) or UEFI boot mode (Windows).

Under the st1 and sc1 small read/write inefficiency section, the quote states an I/O of 1 MiB or less counts as a 1 MiB I/O credit and sequential I/Os merge into 1 MiB blocks counting as one 1 MiB credit.

The second quote says st1 and sc1 are optimized for sequential I/O and discourage small random I/O; the first quote, which recommends gp SSD or Provisioned IOPS SSD instead, appears word for word under both the st1 and the Cold HDD headings (corpus search).
